title: == versus ===, Object.is, and SameValueZero
hook: Three equality notions exist in JavaScript: loose `==` with coercion, strict `===` without, and `SameValueZero` used by `Map`/`Set`. Pick the right one or your cache keys and NaN checks break.

blocks.text: **Strict equality (`===`)** compares type and value without coercion — the default choice in modern code. **Loose equality (`==`)** applies the Abstract Equality Comparison algorithm: it may convert types (e.g. `'5' == 5` → `true`) before comparing. **`Object.is(a, b)`** uses **SameValue**: like `===` but treats `NaN` as equal to `NaN` and distinguishes `+0` from `-0`. **`SameValueZero`** (used internally by `Map`/`Set`) is like `Object.is` but treats `+0` and `-0` as equal.

entries.plainDefinition: Compares without type conversion. Different types always false. Same reference for objects.
Compares with coercion. `'5' == 5` → `true`. `null == undefined` → `true`. Avoid in new code.
Like === but NaN equals NaN and +0 equals -0. Used by Map/Set key lookup.

blocks.text: `==` causes subtle bugs: `userInput == 0` is true for `''`, `false`, and `'0'`. Production code uses `===` and explicit parsing. `Map` and `Set` use SameValueZero — so `NaN` keys work, and `+0`/`-0` collapse. `Object.is` is the right tool for `NaN` checks and distinguishing signed zeros in math libraries. C# `==` on value types compares values; on reference types it compares references unless overloaded — no cross-type coercion like JavaScript.

blocks.title: Default to ===
blocks.body: ESLint `eqeqeq` enforces `===` except `value == null` (checks both null and undefined in one expression). Parse types at boundaries; do not let `==` coerce for you.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Same type → compare like ===
items.body: Two numbers, two strings, etc. — no conversion needed.

items.title: null == undefined → true
items.body: The only case where `==` is idiomatic: `x == null` catches both null and undefined.

diagram.title: Three equality algorithms
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  subgraph strict ["=== (Strict Equality)"]
    S1["Same type required"]
    S2["NaN !== NaN"]
    S3["+0 === -0"]
  end
  subgraph loose ["== (Abstract Equality)"]
    L1["Coerce types first"]
    L2["null == undefined"]
    L3["'5' == 5 → true"]
  end
  subgraph svz ["SameValueZero / Object.is"]
    Z1["NaN equals NaN"]
    Z2["Object.is: +0 !== -0"]
    Z3["Map/Set: +0 == -0"]
  end

snippet.label: == coercion classics
snippet.code:
console.log('5' == 5);      // true — string → number
console.log(0 == false);      // true — false → 0
console.log('' == false);     // true — both → 0
console.log(null == undefined); // true — special rule
console.log([] == false);     // true — [] → '' → 0
console.log([1] == 1);        // true — [1] → '1' → 1

// Same with ===:
console.log('5' === 5);       // false — different types
console.log(0 === false);     // false
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–6: `==` coerces until types match or gives up. Line 3: empty string and false both coerce to 0. Lines 9–10: `===` stops coercion — different types are always false.

snippet.label: NaN and signed zero
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–3: `===` fails for NaN; use `Number.isNaN` or `Object.is`. Lines 5–6: only `Object.is` distinguishes +0 and -0. Lines 8–12: Map uses SameValueZero — NaN keys work, ±0 collapse.

snippet.label: Production equality patterns
snippet.explanation: Lines 2–4: strict string compare. Lines 7–9: rare acceptable `==` use. Lines 12–13: deep equality needs a library or recursive compare. Lines 16–18: objects compare by reference with `===`.

snippet.label: Failure mode — == in validation
snippet.explanation: Lines 2–5: `==` treats `''` and `false` as equal to 0. Lines 11–15: explicit parse + `===` removes coercion surprises. Classic production bug in form validation.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `==` for general comparisons. Expecting `===` to compare object contents. Using `isNaN(x)` instead of `Number.isNaN(x)` — `isNaN` coerces first. Not knowing Map/Set use SameValueZero, not `===`.

blocks.text: Know the three algorithms by name: Strict Equality Comparison (`===`), Abstract Equality Comparison (`==`), SameValue (`Object.is`), and SameValueZero (`Map`/`Set`). `Array.prototype.includes` uses SameValueZero — so `arr.includes(NaN)` works but `arr.includes(-0)` finds `+0`. `indexOf` uses Strict Equality — `arr.indexOf(NaN)` is always -1. `Object.is(+0, -0)` is false because IEEE 754 signed zero matters in some math; Map collapses them for practical key lookup. The only widely accepted `==` idiom is `x == null`. Coercion in `==` is fully specified — walk through `[] == ![]` as a whiteboard exercise (true).

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot explain why `'5' == 5` is true but `'5' === 5` is false. Saying `NaN === NaN` is true. Not knowing Map uses SameValueZero. Recommending `==` for general use without mentioning coercion rules.

interviewTakeaways: Default to `===`; use `==` only for `x == null` (null or undefined).
`==` applies Abstract Equality Comparison — coerces types before compare.
`NaN === NaN` is false; use `Number.isNaN()` or `Object.is(NaN, NaN)`.
Map/Set use SameValueZero: NaN keys work; +0 and -0 are equal.
60s: === no coercion. == coerces ('5'==5). Object.is for NaN. Map uses SameValueZero. Default ===.
commonPitfalls: Weak: '== and === are the same for numbers.' Strong: '== coerces types; === requires same type and value.'
Using isNaN(x) — coerces x first; prefer Number.isNaN(x).
Strong answer: '=== default. == only for null check. SameValueZero for Map. Object.is for NaN and ±0.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript ESLint `eqeqeq` recommends `===`. Structural equality is a compile-time concept only — run time still uses reference equality for objects.
C# `==` on reference types compares references unless overloaded. No `'5' == 5` coercion — types must match or convert explicitly.
